docs.title: geomech
docs.text:
Symbolic derivation of equations of motion on smooth manifolds.

geomech uses variational calculus on Lie groups to derive globally valid, singularity-free equations of motion.

docs.title: What it does
docs.text:
Given a Lagrangian and virtual work, geomech automatically derives globally valid, singularity-free equations of motion on Lie groups (\(SO(3)\), \(S^2\)) using Hamilton's principle and variational calculus -- no Euler angles or quaternions required.

The pipeline:

  1. Define symbolic scalars, vectors, and matrices
  2. Build kinetic/potential energy and virtual work expressions
  3. Call compute_eom() -- the library takes the variation of the action, applies the manifold kinematics, simplifies, integrates by parts and extracts the equations (The Pipeline, Stage by Stage)

docs.title: Code generation
docs.text:
geomech.codegen turns the symbolic output of the pipeline into plain numeric functions: the blocks of to_standard_form, the equations of compute_eom, the blocks of linearize and the total energy of a Lagrangian. Every generated function goes through one code path, and the test suite checks it against geomech.numeric.evaluate on every pinned system.

from geomech.codegen import StateLayout, to_source, lambdify, generate_module, energy_function

layout = StateLayout(variables, inputs=[f, M], params=[m, J, g, e3])
src = to_source(expr, layout)                 # one expression -> Python source
fn = lambdify(expr, layout)                   # -> fn(state, u, p, a=None)
generate_module(system, layout, "model.py")   # writes a module, returns its source
E = energy_function(L, layout)                # -> E(state, p)

Two targets:

Target Dependency Use "numpy" (default) numpy only simulation (scipy.integrate.solve_ivp), tests, examples "casadi" extra geomech[casadi] optimal control, automatic derivatives; the generated module imports casadi, geomech does not

A generated module needs only numpy (or casadi and numpy), not geomech.

docs.title: The state layout
docs.text:
StateLayout(variables, inputs=(), params=()) is the single source of truth for how the symbols map to arrays, and is embedded in every generated module as LAYOUT (plain data, StateLayout.to_dict()).

Variable Configuration slot Velocity slot Acceleration s: Scalar (\(\mathbb{R}\)) s (1) ṡ (1) s̈ x: Vector (\(\mathbb{R}^3\)) x (3) ẋ (3) ẍ q: S2 q (3, unit) ω (3, \(\perp q\)) ω̇ R: SO3 R (9, row-major) Ω (3) Ω̇
  • state holds every configuration slot in variable order (the SystemVariables order: scalars, vectors, matrices), then every velocity slot in the same order. layout.slices[str(symbol)] is the slice of a configuration or velocity symbol; layout.accel_slices and layout.input_slices those of a and u.
  • a stacks the accelerations in variable order; it is an argument only of the functions whose expressions contain an acceleration (compute_eom equations, linearization blocks).
  • u stacks the inputs in the order given (a scalar takes 1 entry, a vector 3).
  • Required arguments. A generated function converts (and so requires) only the arrays its expressions use: a when they contain an acceleration, u when they contain an input. Passing None for a required array raises ValueError (u must have 1 entries, got None (u is required here)), and so does a wrong size. A function whose expressions have no input accepts u=None, which is always the case for a system without inputs; likewise a=None (the default of lambdify) without accelerations. The generated code never reads None as zero input. That shorthand belongs to geomech.simulation (accelerations(module, state, u=None, p), simulate(..., u=None)), whose functions document None as zero input; mass, bias, input_matrix and energy take no u at all.
  • p is a dict keyed by str(symbol) of every parameter: for a scalar a Python or NumPy scalar, or a 0-d or single-element array or sequence (converted to a float; more entries raise ValueError naming the parameter); any array of 3 or 3×3 entries for a vector or matrix. A missing key raises KeyError, an extra one ValueError, both naming the key. Numeric literals (0.5, (-1)) and the zero and identity constants are inlined, never parameters. A named scalar with a value (Scalar("m", value=2)) is a symbol, so it is a parameter.
  • collect_params(system, variables, inputs) lists the symbols that the variables and inputs do not cover (sorted by name): the params to pass. Pass what the system is made of: [L, dW] (the usual call), [L] plus the equations, the dict of compute_eom or of to_standard_form, a LinearizedSystem, one expression, or a list of these. The tangent and variation vectors of the variables (ω, ξ, Ω, η, which dW and compute_eom hold) are left out, and StateLayout rejects them as parameters. Anything it cannot walk (a number, a string, an object without symbols) raises TypeError instead of giving [].
  • layout.pack(**slots) builds a flat state from named slot values and layout.unpack(state) splits one (or a (N, n_state) array such as Trajectory.state) into a dict. The names are the slot identifiers below (x_L, q, R, x_L_dot, omega_q, Omega_R); pack also takes a dict keyed by those names or by the printed symbols. Every configuration slot is required, a velocity left out is zero, R is a 3×3 matrix or its 9 row-major entries. pack does not project onto the manifold; simulate and lqr check the state. Velocity names follow the variable's name, indices included: x_dot, omega_q1 for S2("q1"), Omega_R2 for SO3("R2"); layout.slot_names() lists every key in state order.

x_eq = layout.pack(x_L=np.zeros(3), q=[0, 0, -1], R=np.eye(3))   # at rest
layout.unpack(traj.state)["q"]                                    # (N, 3)
layout.slot_names()          # ['x_L', 'q', 'R', 'x_L_dot', 'omega_q', 'Omega_R']
- layout.state_from_env(env), accel_from_env, inputs_from_env, params_from_env convert an Evaluator env (printed-name keys, (3, 1) columns) to the flat arrays, and env_from_arrays(state, a, u, p) converts back. - Each slot also has a Python identifier for the generated code (\omega_{q} → omega_q, ω̇ → omega_q_dot, ẋ → x_dot, ẍ → x_ddot).

Generation checks every leaf: it must be a configuration, velocity, acceleration, input or parameter of the layout, a numeric literal, or a zero or identity constant. A stray leaf, a TimeDerivative of a non-leaf, a Variation or a time integral raises ValueError naming it. Two layout symbols that print alike raise at construction.

docs.title: The generated module
docs.text:
For a standard-form system (to_standard_form):

LAYOUT = {...}                              # StateLayout.to_dict()
def mass(state, p)         -> (n, n_a)      # block matrix of M[a_j] per equation
def bias(state, p)         -> (n,)          # stacked f
def input_matrix(state, p) -> (n, n_u)      # block matrix of G[u_k]
def kinematics(state)      -> (n_config,)   # ṡ, ẋ, ω × q, R hat(Ω) row-major
def energy(state, p)                        # with generate_module(..., lagrangian=L)
def layout()                                # a copy of LAYOUT

so that the equations read mass @ a + bias + input_matrix @ u = 0. Equations (block rows) are in the order of the configuration variables; a scalar equation takes one row and a vector equation three. For compute_eom output the module has residual(state, a, u, p) (the stacked equations E) and kinematics. For a LinearizedSystem it has M_lin, A_lin, B_lin, each (state, a, u, p), with the rows of LinearizedSystem.rows and the columns of dstates, states and inputs; the slices are recorded in LINEARIZATION.

One layout for everything. Generate the standard-form and the linearization module from the same StateLayout, built with the same SystemVariables and the same inputs list (same order) as to_standard_form and linearize. The columns of input_matrix follow the layout's inputs and those of B_lin follow lin.inputs; with a different order the two would pair a column with a different entry of u, and a controller designed on B_lin would act on the wrong channels. generate_module therefore raises ValueError when the variables (rows and states) or inputs of a LinearizedSystem are not those of the layout in the same order, naming both orders, and lqr(..., module=...) checks that the two modules have the same LAYOUT (see Troubleshooting).

examples/generated/ holds the modules of the nine systems of tests/vbl_systems.py (<name>.py from the standard form with energy, <name>_lin.py from linearize). python scripts/regenerate_generated.py rewrites them (and deletes the files of systems no longer listed); --check writes nothing and exits 1 when a module is out of date or missing, when a stale file is left over, or when a generated file is not tracked by git. CI runs --check.

docs.title: Worked example: the spherical pendulum
docs.text:
Lee et al. Eq. 5.14, \(L = \tfrac12 m l^2\,\omega\cdot\omega - m g l\, q\cdot e_3\) and \(\delta W = \xi\cdot f\):

import numpy as np
from geomech import S2, Dot, Scalar, SystemVariables, Vector, compute_eom, getScalars
from geomech import to_standard_form
from geomech.codegen import StateLayout, generate_module, load_module

m, g, l = getScalars("m g l", attr=["Constant"])
e3 = Vector("e3", attr=["Constant"])
q, f = S2("q"), Vector("f")
omega, xi = q.get_tangent_vector(), q.get_variation_vector()
half = Scalar("0.5", value=0.5, attr=["Constant"])
L = half * m * l * l * Dot(omega, omega) - m * g * l * Dot(q, e3)
variables = SystemVariables(vectors=[q])

eom = compute_eom(L, Dot(xi, f), variables)
sf = to_standard_form(eom, variables, inputs=[f])
layout = StateLayout(variables, inputs=[f], params=[e3, g, l, m])
src = generate_module(sf, layout, "spherical_pendulum.py", lagrangian=L)

state is [q (3), ω (3)], a is [ω̇ (3)], u is [f (3)]. The generated functions (from examples/generated/spherical_pendulum_s2.py):

def mass(state, p):
    """Mass matrix M(state): blocks M[a_j] per equation (M = -physical inertia)."""
    _check_params(p, _PARAMS)
    l = _scalar(p["l"], "l")
    m = _scalar(p["m"], "m")
    out = np.zeros((3, 3))
    out[0:3, 0:3] = np.eye(3) * (m * l * l * -1)
    return out


def bias(state, p):
    """Bias f(state): the terms of each equation free of accelerations and inputs."""
    _check_params(p, _PARAMS)
    state = _arr(state, 6, "state")
    q = state[0:3]
    e3 = _vec(p["e3"])
    g = _scalar(p["g"], "g")
    l = _scalar(p["l"], "l")
    m = _scalar(p["m"], "m")
    out = np.zeros(3)
    out[0:3] = _cross(q, e3) * (m * g * l * -1)
    return out


def energy(state, p):
    """Total energy E = sum((dL/dv) . v) - L at the state."""
    ...
    _t0 = m * l * l * (omega_q @ omega_q)
    return _t0 * 0.5 + m * g * l * (q @ e3)

Used directly:

mod = load_module("spherical_pendulum.py")   # or: import spherical_pendulum as mod
p = {"e3": [0, 0, 1], "g": 9.81, "l": 1.0, "m": 1.0}
q0 = np.array([np.sin(0.3), 0.0, np.cos(0.3)])
state = np.concatenate([q0, [0.0, 0.5, 0.0]])          # ω ⊥ q
M, f = mod.mass(state, p), mod.bias(state, p)
mod.energy(state, p)                                     # ½ m l² |ω|² + m g l q·e₃

docs.title: Translation and conventions
docs.text:
Each node class maps to one construct; vectors are (3,) arrays and matrices (3, 3) (CasADi: 3×1 columns and 3×3).

Node NumPy CasADi Note Add/VAdd/MAdd a + b + … same Mul/SVMul/SMMul a * s same scalar times anything MVMul M @ v ca.mtimes(M, v) a row vᵀM is generated as Mᵀv MMMul A @ B ca.mtimes(A, B) VVMul inner a @ b, outer np.outer(a, b) ca.dot, ca.mtimes(a, b.T) by is_row_vector Dot a @ b ca.dot(a, b) Cross _cross(a, b) ca.cross(a, b) NumPy: component-wise helper, same values as np.cross at a fraction of its per-call cost Hat / Vee _hat(v) / _vee(M) same helpers emitted once per module Transpose M.T; of a vector, the vector same TimeDerivative of a leaf its velocity or acceleration slot same anything else raises zero / identity 0.0, np.zeros(3), np.zeros((3, 3)), np.eye(3) ca.DM.zeros, ca.DM.eye(3) ±inf / nan literal np.inf, -np.inf, np.nan ca.inf, -ca.inf, np.nan inlined, never a parameter
  • Rows. There is one vector type; a row (is_row_vector) is generated as the same 3-vector as its column, and the structure only decides between the inner and the outer product of a VVMul and the side of a row MVMul. A scalar equation's block for a vector acceleration (or input, or linearization column) fills a 1×3 block of the matrix.
  • Common subexpressions. A subtree that occurs more than once is computed once into a local _tN; long expressions are split into locals so that every line is short. Nothing else is simplified. Subtrees are compared structurally (a leaf by its str, the engine's identity; an operation by its class and operands), with the identity of each node object computed once per function, so generation time is linear in the number of node objects, also for trees that reuse a subtree many times.
  • Signs. Those of Conventions: M is −(physical inertia) in the standard form (mass of a point mass is −m I), and the linearization blocks have the positive inertia (M δẋ = A δx + B δu).
  • Values. The CasADi functions take NumPy arrays or CasADi expressions (SX, MX, DM) for state, a, u and the values of p and return CasADi objects, so ca.Function and ca.jacobian apply to them directly.

docs.title: The S² mass block
docs.text: An S² equation is meaningful only on the tangent plane, (I − qqᵀ) E = 0 (Conventions), and the module returns the blocks as derived, not projected. Depending on the Lagrangian the S² mass block is singular (rank 2: Hat(q) Hat(q) m_Q l² in the quadrotor with a suspended load) or full rank (−m l² I for the spherical pendulum, where the engine already used q · ω̇ = 0). Either way the unprojected 3×3 solve is not the equation of motion: the generated module does not solve for the accelerations. Replace each S² block row by P_q · row (with P_q = I − qqᵀ) plus a multiple s q qᵀ on its own ω̇ column (s = the tangent inertia, see Simulation) and its right-hand side by −P_q (bias + G u); the system is then square and full rank and its solution satisfies q · ω̇ = 0. geomech.simulation.accelerations does exactly this (Simulation).

docs.title: Total energy
docs.text: energy_function(L, layout) returns E(state, p) = Σ (∂L/∂v)·v − L over the velocities ṡ, ẋ, ω, Ω, generated through the same code path (energy_expr gives the expression, momenta the ∂L/∂v). ∂L/∂v is derived with the engine: the first variation δL is expanded, its terms are split by perturbation symbol as linearize does, and extract_linear_coeff gives the coefficient of each velocity perturbation (d/dt(δs), d/dt(δx), δω, δΩ). Σ (∂L/∂v)·v is the derivative of L(q, λv) at λ = 1, which does not depend on the velocity coordinates as long as they are linear in the rates (q̇ = ω × q, Ṙ = R Ω̂), so E = L₂ − L₀ is the energy of Lee et al. The tests compare ∂L/∂v with a finite difference of the generated Lagrangian, E with a finite difference in λ, and check dE/dt = 0 along the unforced dynamics of the nine systems of tests/vbl_systems.py.

docs.title: Conventions
docs.text: The choices below are fixed by the code; each one has surprised someone reading an equation. Equation numbers refer to Lee et al., Global Formulations of Lagrangian and Hamiltonian Dynamics on Manifolds.

docs.title: Signs
docs.text:
E = −(Euler–Lagrange) + forcing. compute_eom returns, for each variation vector, the coefficient E of that variation in the integrand of δS after integration by parts, and the equation is E = 0. For L(x, ẋ) and δW = δx·f this is

E = −(d/dt ∂L/∂ẋ − ∂L/∂x) + f,

so the point mass L = ½ m ẋ·ẋ with δW = δx·F gives E = −m ẍ + F, and the free rigid body gives E = −J Ω̇ − Ω × JΩ + M (Eq. 6.16 with every term moved to one side).

M = −(physical inertia) in to_standard_form. The blocks split the same E: E = M a + f + G u, so M[ẍ] = −m I for the point mass, M[Ω̇] = −J for a rigid body, and G[F] = I for a force entering as δx·F.

VBL. linearize takes δE and defines its blocks so that the physical inertia is positive: δE = −M δv̇ + A δx + B δu, i.e. M[δv̇] = −coeff(δv̇, δE), and the result reads M δẋ = A δx + B δu (Variation-Based Linearization).

docs.title: S² equations live on the tangent plane
docs.text: For a point q ∈ S² the variation is δq = ξ × q with ξ ⊥ q, so only the part of E orthogonal to q is an equation: (I − q qᵀ) E = 0. E as derived in general has a component along q (from the forcing, from ω × c, from A ω̇), and to_standard_form and linearize return the terms as derived, not projected. To integrate, solve (I − qqᵀ)(M ω̇ + f + Σ G u) = 0 together with ω̇ ⊥ q; the unprojected 3×3 solve gives q·ω̇ ≠ 0 and a trajectory that leaves the sphere. numeric.check_eom compares on the tangent plane for the same reason.

docs.title: Rows and columns
docs.text:
There is one VECTOR type; a row is recognised by its structure (is_row_vector): Transpose(column), a row times a matrix vᵀM (MVMul(row, M)), a scalar multiple of a row, a sum whose first addend is a row, and d/dt, δ, ∫ of a row.

  • s * v.T() builds SVMul(vᵀ, s), printed (v)'*s; v.T() * s builds Transpose(SVMul(v, s)), printed (v*s)'. Both are the same row; simplify rewrites (s vᵀ) w to s (vᵀ w), but (vᵀ s) w and s (vᵀ w) are not merged yet.
  • v.T() * w is the inner product (VVMul, a scalar), v * w.T() the outer product (a matrix). Integration by parts works on Dot; collect turns an inner product holding the velocity of a variation vector into a Dot, so v.T() * A * v / 2 in a kinetic energy derives (tested for ½ ẋᵀAẋ and ½ ΩᵀJΩ, which gives the same string as ½ Ω·JΩ). Dot(v, A * v) is still the form the rest of the engine knows best: prefer it when there is a choice.
  • Dot, Cross and Hat take columns; Dot(a.T(), b), Cross(a, b.T()), Hat(a.T()) and a sum mixing a row and a column (a.T() + b) are still built (existing code constructs them) but check_tree rejects them.

docs.title: Zeros, numbers and folding
docs.text:
• Zero leaves. Zero prints 0, ZeroVector prints 0v, ZeroMatrix prints 0; Number(0) prints (0) and is flagged zero. Transpose(ZeroVector) ((0v)') is the zero row that linearize uses for an empty scalar-row × vector-column block. The variation and the derivative of a Constant symbol are the zero leaves of its type (Zero, ZeroVector, ZeroMatrix; a vector or matrix of a size other than 3 or 3×3 gets a zero leaf of its own size). geomech.core.base.constants has zero_like(expr) and negate(expr) for code that builds trees.
  • 0 + x is x for every type, so sum([a, b, c]) works for vectors and matrices. x + 0 keeps the zero until simplify for a scalar (m + 0 prints (m+(0))), and is an error for a vector or a matrix (0 is a scalar: VAdd cannot combine VECTOR 'x' and SCALAR '(0)'); write x + ZeroVector or leave the zero out.
  • Products. Every product node prints its two factors joined by *: Mul (m*l), SVMul (x*m), SMMul (J*(2)), MVMul (J*\Omega), MMMul (R*J), VVMul ((a)'*b, a*(b)'). Before phase 5b the factors were juxtaposed, so Mul(ab, c) and Mul(a, bc) both printed abc and compared equal. repr keeps · between factors and * as the constant marker.
  • Numbers. Number(2.5) prints (2.5), Number(-1) (-1); x * -1 and -x are SVMul(x, (-1)), printed x*(-1). A scalar factor is always normalised to the right of SVMul/SMMul (m * x is SVMul(x, m), printed x*m). simplify multiplies the numeric factors of a product chain into one number placed last (Mul(-0.5, Mul(m, 2)) → Mul(m, -1), (-1)*m*l*l → m*l*l*(-1)); a float with an integer value becomes an int (0.5 · 2 · (-1) prints (-1), not (-1.0), and a bare Number(2.0) simplifies to (2)), and every number literal is written the way Number writes it (Scalar("0.5", value=0.5) simplifies to (0.5)), so every equation prints its coefficients the same way. Numeric addends are summed.
  • Like terms. Two addends merge when, after flattening their products, they have the same vector or matrix base and the same symbolic factors as a multiset; their numbers are added: x*(2)*y + x*y*(3) → x*y*(5), v a − v a → 0, (vᵀw)s + s(vᵀw) → (vᵀw)*s*(2) ((vᵀ s) w is first pulled to (vᵀ w) s). Addends with different symbolic coefficients are not factored (x a + x b stays). Scalar products, Dot and the inner product of two columns are treated as commutative (aᵀb s − bᵀa s is 0); bases and factors built with MMMul, MVMul, Cross, SVMul, SMMul or an outer product are compared operand by operand, so A B v s − B A v s and (a×b) m + (b×a) m are not merged. Grouping is one pass, keyed by geomech.core.transformations.simplification.term_key.
  • Float cancellation. Like terms are merged by their numeric coefficients; a sum whose magnitude is at most 1e-12 times the largest coefficient that went into it is treated as an exact zero (_CANCEL_RTOL in simplification.py): x*0.1*3 − x*0.3 is 0, not x(5.55e-17).
  • A named number. Scalar("(-1)") without value prints exactly like Number(-1) but is a symbol; check_tree rejects it. Scalar("m", value=2) is a symbol with a value: every simplification keeps it by name (m + m is m*(2), never (4); with l = Scalar("l", value=3), m·l stays m*l, never (6)), to_latex prints m, and only geomech.numeric (Evaluator, evaluate, check_eom) uses the 2. A number literal is a scalar leaf printed as its own value: Number(2), Zero, One, Scalar("0.5", value=0.5) and the numbers the operators wrap (2 * x); geomech.core.base.expressions.is_number_literal tells them apart.

docs.title: str is the identity
docs.text:
a == b is type(a) is type(b) and str(a) == str(b), plus, for a calculus node (Variation, TimeDerivative, TimeIntegral), the classes of the nodes down to its first non-calculus operand; hashing uses str. expr.has(x) uses the same ==. Hence:

  • two leaves with the same printed name are the same symbol, whatever their flags (Scalar("k", attr=["Constant"]) == Scalar("k")), so J2 = Matrix("J1") silently merges two inertias, and two S2("q") objects are the same point;
  • leaves of different classes differ even with one name: Scalar("x") != Vector("x"), Variation(Scalar("x")) != Variation(Vector("x")), Transpose(Vector("x")) != Transpose(Matrix("x")), and Scalar("m") does not occur in Dot(Vector("m"), w);
  • products print a * between their factors, and * is reserved for that: a symbol name may not contain it (Scalar("m*l") raises ValueError; write ml, or x^\ast for a superscript star). Every * in a printed form is therefore a product boundary, so two products print alike only when they multiply factors that print alike, in the same order: Mul(ab, c) is ab*c and Mul(a, bc) is a*bc, but the regroupings (a*b)*c and a*(b*c) both print a*b*c and are equal (they have one value);
  • commutative rearrangements are different trees (a*b vs b*a), so like-term merging uses a structural key (term_key) that knows Dot, Mul and inner products commute, and a few equivalent terms are not merged;
  • nodes are frozen dataclasses with tuple operands: a tree cannot change after it is built (assignment raises FrozenInstanceError), so a node can be shared between trees and used as a dictionary key; pickling and copy.deepcopy work;
  • the pinned tests compare str of every equation byte for byte. repr is the readable debugging form (leaf kinds v:x, M:J, S2:q, SO3:R, a trailing * for a constant, · for products) and is not an identity.

docs.title: Glossary
docs.text:
• configuration variable: A leaf listed in SystemVariables: a Scalar, a Vector, an S2 point or an SO3 point. Hamilton's principle varies it; each one gets an equation.
  • tangent vector: The velocity coordinate of a manifold point: ω_q for S2("q") (q̇ = ω × q, ω ⊥ q) and Ω_R for SO3("R") (Ṙ = R Hat(Ω), body frame). Obtained with q.get_tangent_vector(); a TS2/TSO3 leaf that remembers its point.
  • variation vector: The free variation of a configuration variable, whose coefficient is the equation: δx for a Scalar/Vector, ξ_q for S2 (δq = ξ × q, ξ ⊥ q) and η_R for SO3 (δR = R Hat(η)). The keys of the compute_eom result are the printed variation vectors. Used on the EOM side.
  • perturbation: A variable of the linearization (VBL side): the configuration perturbations (δx, ξ, η), the velocity perturbations (δẋ, δω, δΩ), their derivatives and the input variations δu. They are the columns of M, A, B.
  • params: Prescribed time-varying symbols declared with compute_eom(..., params=[l]): their rate (l̇) appears in the equations, their variation is not free and is dropped. to_standard_form accepts them; linearize does not yet.
  • inputs: The forces and torques passed to to_standard_form/linearize (inputs=[f, M]): G (standard form) and B (linearization) are their coefficients. For compute_eom they are ordinary non-constant symbols in δW. An input must be the same symbol as its leaf in the equations (class, attr, size): Scalar("g") against a constant Scalar("g", attr=["Constant"]) raises ValueError, as does a param of compute_eom. Both functions, and StateLayout, accept and reject the same inputs (check_inputs): an ordered sequence (a list, tuple or generator) of distinct non-constant Scalar/Vector leaves that are neither a configuration variable, a tangent or variation vector (ω, ξ, Ω, η), nor printed like a velocity, an acceleration or any other node of the equations; inputs=None means none. A set or a dict raises TypeError: the order of inputs is the order of the columns of B and of the generated u vector, and a set has no order (it would depend on the hash seed). A size may be spelled 3, [3] or (3,): leaves store it as a tuple. A param of compute_eom may also be an input only while its rate does not occur in the equations (AlgebraicError otherwise).
  • constant: A leaf with attr=["Constant"] (or a number): its variation and derivative vanish. A symbol that is neither a configuration variable, a param nor a constant makes compute_eom raise (Troubleshooting).

docs.title: Point mass
docs.text:
Derives Newton's equation \(m\ddot{x} = f - mge_3\) for a particle in a gravitational field.

from geomech import *
import numpy as np

m, g = getScalars('m g', attr=['Constant'])
e3 = Vector('e3', attr=['Constant'], value=np.array([0., 0., 1]))
x, f = getVectors(['x', 'f'])

v = x.t_diff()

KE = m * Dot(v, v) * 0.5
PE = m * x.dot(g * e3)
L  = KE - PE

dW = Dot(x.delta(), f)

eqs = compute_eom(L, dW, SystemVariables(vectors=[x]))
print_eom(eqs)

docs.title: Spherical pendulum on \(S^2\)
docs.text:
A point mass constrained to the surface of a sphere. The attitude \(q \in S^2\) is a unit vector -- no angles, no singularities.

from geomech import *
import numpy as np

m, g, l = getScalars('m g l', attr=['Constant'])
e3 = Vector('e3', attr=['Constant'], value=np.array([0., 0., 1]))

q = S2('q')             # attitude on the 2-sphere
f = Vector('f')

x = l * q
v = x.t_diff()

KE = m * Dot(v, v) * 0.5
PE = m * x.dot(g * e3)
L  = KE - PE
dW = Dot(q.delta(), f)

eqs = compute_eom(L, dW, SystemVariables(vectors=[q]))
print_eom(eqs)

The library automatically uses the \(S^2\) variation formula \(\delta q = \xi \times q\) and time derivative \(\dot{q} = \omega \times q\) to produce the globally valid equations.

docs.title: Rigid body on \(SO(3)\)
docs.text:
A rigid body with rotation matrix \(R \in SO(3)\), body-frame inertia \(J\), and center of mass offset \(\rho\).

from geomech import *
import numpy as np

J = Matrix('J', attr=['Constant', 'SymmetricMatrix'])
rho = Vector('\\rho', attr=['Constant'])
m, g = getScalars('m g', attr=['Constant'])
e3 = Vector('e_3', attr=['Constant'], value=np.array([0., 0., 1]))

R = SO3('R')             # rotation matrix on SO(3)
Om = R.get_tangent_vector()
eta = R.get_variation_vector()
M = Vector('M')          # external torque

x = R * rho
v = x.t_diff()

KE = Dot(Om, J * Om) * 0.5 + Dot(v, v) * m * 0.5
PE = m * g * Dot(x, e3)
L  = KE - PE
dW = Dot(eta, M)

eqs = compute_eom(L, dW, SystemVariables(matrices=[R]))
print_eom(eqs)

The \(SO(3)\) variation \(\delta R = R\hat{\eta}\) and kinematics \(\dot{R} = R\hat{\Omega}\) are applied automatically.

docs.title: Double rigid pendulum
docs.text:
Two rigid bodies connected in series -- demonstrates multi-body systems.

from geomech import *
import numpy as np

J1 = Matrix('J1', attr=['Constant', 'SymmetricMatrix'])
J2 = Matrix('J2', attr=['Constant', 'SymmetricMatrix'])
rho1 = Vector('\\rho1', attr=['Constant'])
rho2 = Vector('\\rho2', attr=['Constant'])
l1 = Vector('l1', attr=['Constant'])
m1, m2, g = getScalars('m1 m2 g', attr=['Constant'])
e3 = Vector('e_3', attr=['Constant'], value=np.array([0., 0., 1]))

M1, M2 = getVectors('M1 M2')
R1, R2 = SO3('R1'), SO3('R2')
Om1, eta1 = R1.get_tangent_vector(), R1.get_variation_vector()
Om2, eta2 = R2.get_tangent_vector(), R2.get_variation_vector()

x1 = R1 * rho1
x2 = R1 * l1 + R2 * rho2
v2 = x2.t_diff()

KE = (Dot(Om1, J1 * Om1) * 0.5
    + Dot(Om2, J2 * Om2) * 0.5
    + Dot(v2, v2) * m2 * 0.5)
PE = m1 * g * Dot(R1 * rho1, e3) + m2 * g * Dot(R2 * rho2, e3)
L = KE - PE

dW = Dot(eta1, M1) + Dot(eta2, M2)

eqs = compute_eom(L, dW, SystemVariables(matrices=[R1, R2]))
print_eom(eqs)

docs.title: Installation
docs.text:
Requires Python >= 3.10.

pip install -e .

docs.title: Your first derivation
docs.text:
Let's derive Newton's equation of motion for a 3D point mass.

from geomech import *
import numpy as np

# Constants
m, g = getScalars('m g', attr=['Constant'])
e3 = Vector('e3', attr=['Constant'], value=np.array([0., 0., 1]))

# State variables
x, f = getVectors(['x', 'f'])
v = x.t_diff()

# Energies
KE = m * Dot(v, v) * 0.5
PE = m * x.dot(g * e3)
L  = KE - PE

# Virtual work
dW = Dot(x.delta(), f)

# Derive EOM
eqs = compute_eom(L, dW, SystemVariables(vectors=[x]))
print_eom(eqs)

This produces the equation \(m \ddot{x} = f - mge_3\), output as a LaTeX integral equation.

Every symbol in L and dW is one of three things: a configuration variable (listed in SystemVariables), a constant (attr=["Constant"]), or a prescribed time-varying parameter declared with compute_eom(L, dW, variables, params=[l]) — a cable length l(t), say, whose rate l̇ appears in the equations but whose variation is not free. A symbol that is none of these and whose variation survives (a forgotten y, an e3 missing Constant) raises ValueError naming it; the terms are never dropped silently.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
The compute_eom pipeline, in the order the code runs it:

δS = δL + δW → manifold rules (δω, δΩ) → full_simplify → integration by parts (expand, full_simplify, then per variation vector: collect → IBP → full_simplify) → expand → extract the coefficient of each variation vector → full_simplify.

  1. Variation -- \(\delta L\) by the product rule; manifold points are eager (\(\delta R = R\hat{\eta}\) for \(SO(3)\), \(\delta q = \xi \times q\) for \(S^2\)), and \(\delta S = \delta L + \delta W\)
  2. Manifold rules -- \(\delta\omega = \dot\xi - 2\,\omega \times \xi\) on \(S^2\), \(\delta\Omega = \dot\eta + \Omega \times \eta\) on \(SO(3)\)
  3. Simplify -- expand once, then pull scalars, apply vector identities (orthogonality, unit norm, tangency) and eliminate zeros until nothing changes
  4. Integrate by parts -- for each variation vector, collect rotates every term so its time derivative is the left operand of a Dot, then moves the derivative off it
  5. Expand -- distributes products over sums
  6. Extract -- the coefficient of each variation vector, simplified, is its equation

The Pipeline, Stage by Stage describes each stage and how to see it (compute_eom(..., trace=EOMTrace())); Troubleshooting lists the error messages and the debugging switches; Conventions the sign and printing conventions.

docs.title: Expression types
docs.text:
Type Description Constructor Scalar Symbolic scalar Scalar('m', attr=['Constant']) Vector Column vector (default 3x1) Vector('x') Matrix Square matrix (default 3x3) Matrix('J', attr=['Constant']) S2 Unit vector on the 2-sphere S2('q') SO3 Rotation matrix on \(SO(3)\) SO3('R')

Attributes are passed as a list of strings, attr=['Constant'], and the names are case-sensitive ('constant' raises ValueError listing the valid names).

Batch constructors: getScalars('a b c'), getVectors(['x', 'y']), getMatrices('M N').

docs.title: Operations
docs.text:
Arithmetic -- natural Python operators build expression trees:

a * b          # scalar multiplication
a * x          # scalar-vector multiplication
M * x          # matrix-vector multiplication
x + y          # vector addition
Dot(x, y)      # dot product
Cross(x, y)    # cross product
Hat(x)         # hat map (R^3 -> so(3))
Vee(M)         # vee map (so(3) -> R^3)
Transpose(x)   # transpose (x.T() is the same; Transpose(Transpose(x)) is x)
R.T() * x      # a transposed matrix multiplies like a matrix: R^T x
x.T() * y      # row times column: the inner product x^T y; x * y.T() is the outer product
x.T() * K * x  # a row times a matrix is a row: the quadratic form x^T K x
# (also in a kinetic energy, v.T() * K * v: collect turns it into Dot(v, K * v) for integration by parts)
2 * x, a + 1, 1 - a, -x, x / 2   # numbers on either side (a number adds only to a scalar); / divides by a number only

A mistyped operand raises ExpressionMismatchError naming both operands, e.g. Dot cannot combine SCALAR 'm' and VECTOR 'x'.

Calculus:

x.t_diff()       # time derivative d/dt
x.t_integrate()  # time integral
x.delta()        # variation (delta)

Transformations:

expand(expr)        # distribute products over sums
simplify(expr)      # pull scalars, apply identities, eliminate zeros
full_simplify(expr) # expand + simplify until convergence

Printing -- str(expr) is the internal form and the equality key (products print * between their factors: m*g*Dot(e3,x)); for reading:

to_latex(expr)      # LaTeX, parenthesised where juxtaposition would be ambiguous
print_eom(eqs)      # one LaTeX integral equation per variable (via to_latex)
repr(expr)          # compact: v:x vector, M:J matrix, S2:q, SO3:R; trailing * = constant;
                    # products joined by ·, e.g. m*·g*·<v:e3*, v:x>
print_tree(expr)    # one node per line with every leaf's flags (style="topdown" for a sketch)

docs.title: Manifold Rules: Derivation
docs.text: The kinematic substitutions of pipeline stage 2 (Pipeline), why the S² rule has a factor 2, and how the manifold points are kept out of the tree.

docs.title: S² variation rule: δω = ξ̇ − 2 ω × ξ
docs.text:
manifold_rules.py substitutes Variation(ω) for an S² tangent vector ω by

δω = ξ̇ − 2 ω × ξ

docs.title: Derivation
docs.text:
The kinematics are q̇ = ω × q with ω ⊥ q (equivalently ω = q × q̇) and the variation is δq = ξ × q with ξ ⊥ q. Lee et al. eq. (5.13) give

δω = −S(ω) ξ + (I − q qᵀ) ξ̇ = ξ̇ − ω × ξ − q (q · ξ̇).

The last term does not vanish. Differentiating the constraint ξ · q = 0 along the curve,

q · ξ̇ = −ξ · q̇ = −ξ · (ω × q) = q · (ω × ξ),

and since ω and ξ both lie in the tangent plane, ω × ξ is parallel to q, so q (q · ξ̇) = q (q · (ω × ξ)) = ω × ξ. On the constraint set therefore

δω = ξ̇ − 2 ω × ξ.

δω is not tangent to the sphere: q · δω = −q · ξ̇ = −q · (ω × ξ), which is what keeps δ(ω · q) = 0.

docs.title: History and symptom
docs.text: Until the 2026-11 audits the rule was δω = ξ̇ − ω × ξ, which is only the tangential projection (I − q qᵀ) δω. The two agree whenever ∂L/∂ω ⊥ q, which is the case for every Lagrangian that depends on ω only through q̇ = ω × q (all the pendulum examples), so the pinned pendulum equations never changed. The projection is wrong as soon as ∂L/∂ω has a component along q: with L = ½ m l² ω·ω + c·ω − m g l q·e₃ the true equation is −m l² ω̇ + 2 ω × c − m g l q × e₃ + f and the old rule printed ω × c, i.e. gyroscopic terms came out at half strength (likewise for ½ ω·Aω, a rotating frame |ω + W₀|², R³×S² couplings ẋ·ω and S²×SO(3) couplings ω·Ω, ω·(Rᵀe₃)). The regression tests are in tests/test_s2_variation_fix.py; each pinned equation is also checked against the finite-difference Euler–Lagrange oracle in geomech.numeric.

docs.title: SO(3) variation rule
docs.text: For Ṙ = R·Hat(Ω) and δR = R·Hat(η), equating the mixed derivatives d/dt(δR) = δ(Ṙ) gives δΩ = η̇ + Ω × η exactly (Lee et al. eq. 6.9); it has no hidden normal component.

docs.title: How the S² substitution is organised
docs.text:
• S2.t_diff() eagerly returns Cross(ω, q) — the tree never holds TimeDerivative(q).
  • S2.delta() eagerly returns Cross(ξ, q) — the tree never holds Variation(q).
  • manifold_rules substitutes Variation(ω) → ξ̇ − 2 ω × ξ and Variation(Ω) → η̇ + Ω × η. This is the only place these formulas live; TS2/TSO3 carry no substitution of their own.

An equivalent formulation works at the level of q (substituting δ(q̇), q̇ and δq directly and never forming δω). The two are related by the Jacobi identity; the ω-level formulation needs the extra simplification rules below (BAC-CAB, skew-symmetry) because it produces more intermediate cross products.

docs.title: Rules that rely on the manifold structure
docs.text:
The rewrite rules are listed, with the hypothesis each one checks, in the docstrings of their modules; the ones that depend on S² or SO(3) are:

  • vector.dot_tangent_orthogonal (ω·q = 0), vector.dot_unit_norm (q·q = 1), vector.s2_tangent_recovery (q × (a × q) = a), vector.s2_tangent_negated (q × (q × a) = −a) and vector.s2_double_cross (a × (a × q) = −q (a·a)) in vector_identities.py. Tangency is only assumed for a TS2 leaf of the same point (compared by name) and for Cross(·, q); never for d/dt(ω), d/dt(ξ) or the substituted δω, which is correct because δω is not tangent. vector_rules recurses through Add, Mul, VAdd, SVMul and Cross only.
  • simplify.orthogonal_transpose (RᵀR = RRᵀ = I for an SO3 point), simplify.mvmul_hat_to_cross (Hat(v) w = v × w), simplify.transpose_hat_skew (Hat(v)ᵀ = −Hat(v)), simplify.hat_vee_skew (Hat(Vee(X)) = X for skew-symmetric X only) and simplify.vee_hat in simplification.py.
  • expand.hat_over_vadd (Hat(a + b) = Hat(a) + Hat(b)) in expansion.py.
  • collect.strip_rotation (Dot(R a, R b) = Dot(a, b)), collect.peel_matrix (Dot(M f(v), w) = Dot(f(v), Mᵀ w), one matrix layer per step, only when the target is in the vector operand) and collect.triple_product_* (one name per rotation) in collecting.py.

geomech.set_trace(True) logs each firing (Pipeline).

docs.title: Verifying an equation numerically
docs.text:
geomech.numeric evaluates expression trees with numpy and checks the output of compute_eom against a finite-difference Euler–Lagrange residual that does not use the library's variational rules. It is the regression gate for the engine and the quickest way to gain confidence in a derivation for a new system.

from geomech import evaluate, check_eom, assert_eom, Evaluator

docs.title: Leaf values: the key convention
docs.text:
Every leaf of a tree is identified by its printed name, str(leaf). evaluate takes a dictionary from those names to numpy values and returns a float (scalar expression), a (3, 1) array (vector) or a (3, 3) array (matrix):

Leaf Key Value Scalar("m") "m" float Vector("x") "x" (3, 1) array Matrix("J") "J" (3, 3) array velocity x.t_diff() str(TimeDerivative(x)) (3, 1) array acceleration x.t_diff().t_diff() str(TimeDerivative(TimeDerivative(x))) (3, 1) array q = S2("q") "q" unit (3, 1) array ω = q.get_tangent_vector() str(ω) (3, 1) array ⊥ q R = SO3("R") "R" rotation matrix Ω = R.get_tangent_vector() str(Ω) (3, 1) array

Velocities and tangent vectors are leaves of their own: the tree never holds TimeDerivative(q) for a manifold point (q.t_diff() is Cross(ω, q)), and ẋ is a value you supply, not something computed from x. The zero and identity constants are resolved by type and need no key.

Any leaf missing from the dictionary is drawn once from numpy.random.default_rng(seed), respecting the leaf's declared structure (UnitNorm vectors have unit norm, SymmetricMatrix leaves are symmetric, SO3 leaves are rotations, a Scalar with a value takes that value). A Variation symbol has no natural random value and must be given explicitly.

import numpy as np
from geomech import Vector, Cross, Dot, evaluate

x, e3 = Vector("x"), Vector("e3", attr=["Constant"])
v = x.t_diff()
env = {"x": np.array([[1.0], [0.0], [0.0]]),
       str(v): np.array([[0.0], [2.0], [0.0]]),
       "e3": np.array([[0.0], [0.0], [1.0]])}
evaluate(Dot(Cross(x, v), e3), env)   # 2.0

Evaluator(env, rng) is the underlying class; it stores every value it draws in env, so successive calls on the same instance see the same numbers.

docs.title: Checking an equation of motion
docs.text:
from geomech import (S2, Vector, Dot, Scalar, SystemVariables, getScalars,
                     compute_eom, check_eom)

m, g, l = getScalars("m g l", attr=["Constant"])
e3 = Vector("e3", attr=["Constant"])
q, f = S2("q"), Vector("f")
omega, xi = q.get_tangent_vector(), q.get_variation_vector()
half = Scalar("0.5", value=0.5, attr=["Constant"])

L = half * m * l * l * Dot(omega, omega) - m * g * l * Dot(q, e3)
dW = Dot(xi, f)
variables = SystemVariables(vectors=[q])

eom = compute_eom(L, dW, variables)
err = check_eom(L, dW, variables, eom, inputs=[f])
print(err)          # ~1e-7: the equation −m l² ω̇ − m g l (q × e₃) + f = 0 is right
assert err < 1e-5

check_eom returns the worst relative error over trials random trajectory points and over all configuration variables; assert_eom(..., rtol=1e-5) raises an AssertionError naming the variation vector whose equation is wrong. For a system whose parameters are of order one a correct equation scores at finite-difference noise, about 1e-7 (worst 2.3e-7 over the 36 pinned systems and 10 seeds), and a wrong sign or a dropped term scores 0.02 or more (worst over every term of the same systems). The gap is four orders of magnitude for such systems; it is not unconditional, see "Resolution" below.

docs.title: What it computes
docs.text:
compute_eom returns, for each configuration variable, the coefficient \(E\) of its variation vector in \(\delta\!\int L\,dt + \int \delta W\,dt\) after integration by parts, so the equation of motion is \(E = 0\) and \(E = -(\text{Euler–Lagrange}) + \text{forcing}\) (for a point mass, \(E = -m\ddot x + f\)). The oracle evaluates the numeric Lagrangian with Evaluator and forms the Euler–Lagrange residual \(g\) by central differences:

  • \(\mathbb{R}\), \(\mathbb{R}^3\): \(g = \frac{d}{dt}\frac{\partial L}{\partial v} - \frac{\partial L}{\partial q}\), \(E_{\text{true}} = -g + f\);
  • \(S^2\): the constrained Lagrangian \(\tilde L(q, \dot q) = L(q, q \times \dot q)\) on \(|q| = 1\) with \(\dot q = \omega \times q\), \(E_{\text{true}} = -q \times g + f\), compared on the tangent plane only (Lee et al., Chapter 5);
  • \(SO(3)\): the body-frame form \(g = \frac{d}{dt}\frac{\partial L}{\partial \Omega} - \frac{\partial L}{\partial \Omega} \times \Omega - (A - A^\top)^\vee\) with \(A = R^\top \frac{\partial L}{\partial R}\), \(E_{\text{true}} = -g + f\) (Lee et al., Chapter 6).

The forcing \(f\) is inf_work evaluated with the variable's variation set to each basis vector and the other variations zero. \(d/dt\) is a directional derivative along the sampled velocity and acceleration, so nothing is integrated: the library's \(E(q, v, \dot v, u)\) and \(E_{\text{true}}\) must agree at random accelerations, which pins the mass matrix, the velocity terms and the forces at once.

docs.title: Resolution: what a term must be for the check to see it
docs.text:
The error is measured relative to the size of the whole equation, \(\max(1, |P\,E_{\text{true}}|)\). A term \(t\) that is wrong (sign, missing factor) moves the error by \(2|P\,t| / \max(1, |P\,E_{\text{true}}|)\), so it is resolved at rtol only if that quantity exceeds rtol. With parameters of order one every term is resolved by a wide margin. With a large parameter in the equation it is not: a point mass on a spring with Scalar("k", value=1e7) has \(|E_{\text{true}}| \approx 10^7\), the gravity term \(m g\, e_3\) is of order one, a flipped gravity term moves the error by \(\approx 4 \cdot 10^{-7}\), and check_eom returns ~1e-9 for the correct and ~1e-7 for the wrong equation: both pass at 1e-5. The finite-difference noise scales with \(|L|\) as well (it is 6e-3 to 2e-2 in absolute terms for that system at the default step), so this is a limit of the finite-difference oracle, not of the normalisation alone.

assert_eom therefore checks the resolution of every additive term of each equation (its tangent part on \(S^2\)) and raises, naming the term, its size and the resolution rtol · max(1, |E_true|), when a term is unresolved at every trial. Terms parallel to \(q\) or zero on the constraint set have nothing to resolve and are ignored. If you need to accept such an equation on the relative error alone, pass require_resolved=False; the better fix is to keep the parameters symbolic (random, order one) or to scale them so the terms are of comparable size. check_eom reports the relative error only.

docs.title: What it does not verify
docs.text:
• The normal component on \(S^2\). The coefficient of \(\xi \perp q\) is only defined on the tangent plane, so a term such as \(\omega \times (q \times \dot x) = q\,(\omega\cdot\dot x)\) is invisible to the check. This is correct behaviour, not a gap: such a term has no physical content. The same applies to the equation itself: on \(S^2\) the equation E = 0 returned by compute_eom is only meaningful on the tangent plane, \((I - qq^\top)E = 0\). E generally has a component along \(q\) (from the forcing, from \(\omega \times c\), from \(A\dot\omega\), …), so anyone solving E = 0 for \(\dot\omega\), including from the blocks of to_standard_form or linearize, must project: solve \((I - qq^\top)(M\dot\omega + f + G u) = 0\) with \(\dot\omega \perp q\). The unprojected \(3 \times 3\) solve gives \(q \cdot \dot\omega \neq 0\) and a trajectory that leaves the sphere.
  • Anything below finite-difference noise. d/dt ∂L/∂v nests two central differences with the same step, so the noise is about h² + 1e-16 |L| / h²: ~1e-8 for a Lagrangian of order one at the default h=1e-4 (the minimum of the two terms; at h=1e-5 the roundoff term is ~1e-6, within a factor 10 of the gate, and a correct equation can fail it). A term whose tangent part is below the noise cannot be verified by any normalisation; this grey zone always exists, and it widens with |L| (see "Resolution").
  • Unlisted time-varying parameters. A non-constant leaf that is neither a configuration variable nor listed in params is frozen during the check, so a correct equation that contains its rate looks wrong. List it: check_eom(..., params=[l]). compute_eom takes the same params=[l]; without it, the surviving δl is reported as an error rather than dropped, so the two calls declare the prescribed symbols identically.
  • The symbolic form. Two equations that agree numerically are accepted even if one is not simplified; check_eom checks values, the pinned string tests check form.
  • to_standard_form and linearize. The standard-form split is a rearrangement of the same expression; linearizations are checked separately by geomech.numeric.finite_difference_check.

docs.title: Using it on a new system
docs.text:
1. Build L, dW and SystemVariables as usual and call compute_eom.
  2. Call check_eom(L, dW, variables, eom, inputs=[...]). List every prescribed time-varying symbol in params.
  3. If the error is ~1e-7, the equation is right. If it is ~1, use assert_eom to learn which variable's equation is wrong, then compare print_eom(eom) with the textbook form; a wrong equation is an engine bug worth reporting with the Lagrangian that triggers it. If assert_eom reports an unresolved term, the check could not see that term: use parameters of order one.
  4. Pin the system in a test with assert_eom(...) (or assert check_eom(...) < 1e-5 when the parameters are of order one) next to the string assertion on the equation, so the form and the value are both guarded.

docs.title: The Pipeline, Stage by Stage
docs.text:
compute_eom(L, dW, variables) runs the stages below, in this order (this is the order of the code in geomech/dynamics/eom.py; the README, Getting Started and the compute_eom docstring state the same order):

δS = δL + δW → manifold rules → full_simplify → integration by parts (expand, full_simplify, then per variation vector: collect → IBP → full_simplify) → expand → extract the coefficient of each variation vector → full_simplify.

Every stage is a pure function on an expression tree, so each one can be rerun by hand from the previous one. The names in brackets are the stage names of EOMTrace, and the rule names (vector.dot_tangent_orthogonal, …) are the ones logged by the rule trace.

docs.title: Validation (before any stage)
docs.text: compute_eom first checks its inputs and raises a typed error naming the entry: SystemVariables entries (type, constant, duplicate names, tangent vectors and composite expressions listed as variables), params entries, lagrangian/inf_work types, and inf_work holding a time derivative of a variation vector (virtual work must be linear in the variations themselves). See Troubleshooting for the messages. With GEOMECH_DEBUG=1, check_tree also runs on L and dW.

docs.title: 1. Variation [dL], [dW], [dS]
docs.text: L.delta() applies the product rule through the tree. Manifold leaves are eager: q.delta() for an S2 point is ξ × q, R.delta() for an SO3 point is R Hat(η), and the variation of a velocity is built as the time derivative of the variation (x.t_diff().delta() is d/dt(δx)). Tangent vectors (ω, Ω) are leaves at this point, so their variations stay as δω, δΩ. δS is δL + δW (dW=None or 0 means δW = 0).

docs.title: 2. Manifold rules [manifold_rules]
docs.text:
apply_manifold_rules(dS, variables) replaces the variation of each listed tangent vector by its kinematic expansion (rules manifold.s2_variation_omega, manifold.so3_variation_Omega):

  • S²: δω → ξ̇ − 2 ω × ξ (Lee et al. eq. 5.13 on the constraint set ξ ⊥ q; the derivation, and why the factor is 2, is in Manifold Rules: Derivation);
  • SO(3): δΩ → η̇ + Ω × η (Lee et al. eq. 6.9).

A tangent vector is matched by its printed name, so only the points listed in SystemVariables are expanded.

docs.title: 3. Simplify [simplify]
docs.text:
full_simplify runs expand once, then repeats one simplify pass until the printed tree stops changing (at most max_iter=10 passes; hitting the cap emits the RuntimeWarning "no confirmed fixed point after N passes"). One pass is

  1. pull: hoist scalar factors out of products (pull.dot_scaled, pull.mvmul_scaled, …);
  2. vector_rules: geometric identities, bottom up — orthogonality (vector.dot_cross_orthogonal), unit norm (vector.dot_unit_norm), tangency on S² (vector.dot_tangent_orthogonal, vector.s2_tangent_recovery, …). Like pull, it recurses through every node class (one shared rebuild helper), so a rule fires below a Dot operand, an MVMul, a Hat, a Transpose or a calculus node too;
  3. _eliminate: bottom up, zeros, identities and numbers (simplify.mul_fold, simplify.mvmul_hat_to_cross, simplify.orthogonal_transpose, simplify.transpose_symmetric, simplify.transpose_skew, the MMMul associativity simplify.mmmul_reassociate/simplify.mmmul_combine, …). Like terms are merged on flattened products: x*(2)*y + x*y*(3) → x*y*(5), v a − v a → 0, aᵀb s − bᵀa s → 0, and the numbers of a product are folded into one placed last ((-1)*m → m*(-1), (-1.0) → (-1)).

The rules and the hypothesis each needs are listed in the docstrings of geomech.core.transformations.pulling, .vector_identities and .simplification (the modules of the functions pull, vector_rules and simplify).

docs.title: 4. Integration by parts [ibp.prepare], [ibp.collect[t]], [ibp.integrate[t]], [ibp.simplify[t]], [ibp]
docs.text:
integrate_by_parts(dS, targets) takes the time derivative of each variation vector as a target (d/dt(δx), d/dt(ξ_q), d/dt(η_R), in the order scalars, vectors, matrices). It first runs expand and full_simplify ([ibp.prepare]), then for each target in turn:

  1. collect(expr, target) [ibp.collect[t]] rewrites every term so that the target is the left operand of a Dot: commutativity (collect.flip_target_right, collect.flip_mvmul_left, … : one name per call site), the cyclic triple product (collect.triple_product_left, _right, _left_nested, … : one name per rotation), peeling a matrix off the side holding the target, Dot(M f, w) = Dot(f, Mᵀ w) (collect.peel_matrix), stripping a common rotation Dot(R a, R b) = Dot(a, b) (collect.strip_rotation), and turning an inner product written with rows, vᵀ A w, into a Dot (collect.inner_product_to_dot). A target inside the matrix factor of a product (Hat(Ω), Ω cᵀ) cannot be exposed and raises AlgebraicError naming the term;
  2. one IBP pass [ibp.integrate[t]]: a Dot(ẋ, f) → a Dot(−x, ḟ) (ibp.dot), with the product rule when the scalar prefactor a is not constant (ibp.dot_prefactor, whose rate ȧ is logged as ibp.product_rule), and ẋ g → −x ġ for a scalar target in a product (ibp.scalar_factor). Boundary terms are dropped (Hamilton's principle);
  3. full_simplify [ibp.simplify[t]].

A target that collect could not bring into Dot(target, f) survives this stage; the extraction in stage 6 then fails, and compute_eom names the term (see Troubleshooting).

docs.title: 5. Expand [expand]
docs.text: expand distributes every product over sums (expand.dot_over_vadd, expand.mvmul_over_sum, …) and the linear maps Hat and Vee over a sum (expand.hat_over_vadd, expand.vee_over_madd) so that each additive term of δS carries exactly one variation vector as a direct factor.

docs.title: 6. Extraction [raw[ξ]], [equation[ξ]]
docs.text:
For each variation vector, extract_linear_coeff(dS, vec) returns its coefficient by truncating the tree at the variation vector (the coefficient is always a left factor; geomech/core/math/extract.py has the dispatch grid). A term where the variation vector appears twice raises NonLinearError; one where it appears only inside a calculus operator (a surviving d/dt(η)) raises AlgebraicError. The coefficient is then simplified with full_simplify. The result is {str(vec): (vec, E)} with E = 0 the equation of motion (sign convention in Conventions).

Finally, compute_eom checks that no variation symbol of an unlisted symbol is left in δS (a forgotten degree of freedom, a symbol missing Constant) and raises ValueError naming it.

docs.title: After compute_eom
docs.text:
• to_standard_form(eom, variables, inputs) expands each equation, partitions its terms into acceleration, input and remaining terms, and extracts M, G and f (E = M a + f + G u).
  • linearize(eom, variables, inputs) takes the variation δE of each equation, expands it, partitions its terms by the perturbation symbol each carries and extracts the blocks of M δẋ = A δx + B δu (Variation-Based Linearization).

docs.title: Seeing the stages
docs.text:
Pass an EOMTrace (keyword only); it is filled as the pipeline runs, so after an exception it holds every stage up to the failing one:

from geomech import EOMTrace, compute_eom

tr = EOMTrace()
eom = compute_eom(L, dW, variables, trace=tr)
tr.summary()                 # one line per stage: name, node count, start of the repr
tr.show("simplify")          # print_tree(..., style="indent") of one stage
tr.after_ibp                 # the same stages as attributes
tr.ibp["\\frac{d}{dt}(\\eta_{R})"]["collect"]   # per target: collect / integrate / simplify
tr.raw_equations, tr.equations

Two names look alike: the stage "ibp" (tr["ibp"], tr.show("ibp")) is δS after integration by parts, the attribute tr.after_ibp; the attribute tr.ibp is the dict of per-target steps. To print one step, give its stage name: tr.show("ibp.collect[\\frac{d}{dt}(\\eta_{R})]").

The pipeline clears the trace when it starts, so passing the same EOMTrace to a second compute_eom (re-running a notebook cell) keeps only the second run. When the run raises, the trace keeps the stages before the failure, tr.failed_at names the stage that raised (raw[\eta_{R}], ibp.collect[...], validation, stray_check …) and tr.error the exception class; summary() then starts with FAILED at <stage>: <exception> (the stages below ran before it).

For the rigid pendulum (L = ½ Ω·JΩ − m g e₃·Rρ, dW = η·M), tr.summary(chars=70) prints

dL                                        30 nodes  ((<δ(v:\Omega_{R}), M:J*·v:\Omega_{R}> + <v:\Omega_{R}, M:J*·δ(v:\O...
dW                                         3 nodes  <v:\eta_{R}, v:M>
dS                                        33 nodes  ((<δ(v:\Omega_{R}), M:J*·v:\Omega_{R}> + <v:\Omega_{R}, M:J*·δ(v:\O...
manifold_rules                            41 nodes  ((<(d/dt(v:\eta_{R}) + cross(v:\Omega_{R}, v:\eta_{R})), M:J*·v:\Om...
simplify                                  51 nodes  (<d/dt(v:\eta_{R}), M:J*·v:\Omega_{R}>·(0.5) + <cross(v:\Omega_{R},...
ibp.prepare                               51 nodes  (<d/dt(v:\eta_{R}), M:J*·v:\Omega_{R}>·(0.5) + <cross(v:\Omega_{R},...
ibp.collect[\frac{d}{dt}(\eta_{R})]       52 nodes  (<d/dt(v:\eta_{R}), M:J*·v:\Omega_{R}>·(0.5) + <cross(v:\Omega_{R},...
ibp.integrate[\frac{d}{dt}(\eta_{R})]     56 nodes  (<-v:\eta_{R}, M:J*·d/dt(v:\Omega_{R})>·(0.5) + <cross(v:\Omega_{R}...
ibp.simplify[\frac{d}{dt}(\eta_{R})]      43 nodes  (-<v:\eta_{R}, M:J*·d/dt(v:\Omega_{R})> + <cross(v:\Omega_{R}, v:\e...
ibp                                       43 nodes  (-<v:\eta_{R}, M:J*·d/dt(v:\Omega_{R})> + <cross(v:\Omega_{R}, v:\e...
